sources.title: VAG: Dual-Stream Video-Action Generation for Embodied Data Synthesis

sectionsRead: Title, authors, affiliations, version and abstract (p. 1–2)
3. Method; 3.1 Flow Matching; 3.2 Dual-Stream Generation; 3.3 Training (p. 3–5)
omissions: Text extraction does not reconstruct figure images; inspect the retained PDF for figures and equation/table layout.
Separate supplemental material availability has not been fully verified.

All five supplied text chunks were read individually. PDF pages 1–9 and all six final crops were visually inspected; this resolves the figure-image extraction omission for the reviewed PDF. Reference pages 10–13 were read as text.
Identity matches the catalog title and all 13 authors. The title page identifies arXiv:2604.09330v1 [cs.RO], 10 April 2026; no different revision or edition was supplied or compared.
No appendix is present in the supplied 13-page PDF. Separate supplements remain unverified.
Code and external resources were not inspected, and no experiments were reproduced.

synopsis: VAG synthesizes robot videos and action sequences from an initial image and instruction. A video diffusion transformer supplies pooled clean-latent predictions to an action U-Net during synchronized denoising. The evidence supports improved action prediction and simulation replay, plus a small real-robot policy-pretraining benefit. It does not establish guaranteed alignment or general closed-loop control.

problem.text: Generated robot videos lack the paired motor trajectories needed for policy learning. The authors target this data bottleneck with joint video–action synthesis, arguing that generating a complete video before regressing actions introduces inconsistency and cumulative errors. Their objective is useful training pairs, with direct trajectory replay as an additional application.

contributions.text: A flow-matching framework couples a pretrained video transformer and an action U-Net through synchronized denoising, producing both modalities during the same generation process.
Nonlearnable adaptive 3D pooling turns each predicted clean video latent into global action-conditioning information; the training connection is detached.
Experiments connect prediction quality to simulation replay and downstream policy training, while real-robot VAG replay is illustrated through selected examples.

inputs: Initial RGB camera frame and textual instruction at inference
Paired videos and action trajectories for training; video-derived instructions
outputs: Generated RGB video V with T frames
Aligned action sequence A with T rows and embodiment-specific dimension D

steps.name: Generate a conditional video latent
steps.detail: Cosmos-Predict2 supplies the video DiT. The initial image is a latent prefix; T5-XXL text embeddings enter through cross-attention with classifier-free guidance. Video noise is scaled by the paper's weight sigma. Each denoising step predicts a clean latent, and the final latent is decoded to video.

steps.name: Compress video context into action conditioning
steps.detail: Adaptive 3D pooling averages the clean latent over space and time, retaining one value per latent channel. The vector is repeated to form the global embedding and concatenated with the encoded diffusion timestep for a modified Diffusion Policy 1D U-Net. This transfers video information to actions without an inverse-dynamics stage.

steps.name: Synchronize the two denoisers
steps.detail: Both streams use the same noise intensity during training and synchronized denoising during generation. The U-Net consumes the current video prediction, so the coupling is directional. There is no action-to-video feedback in this version, as the authors explicitly acknowledge.

training.text: Qwen2.5-VL extracts instructions from training videos. A VAE tokenizer compresses time, height and width by 4×8×8; Figure 3 marks the encoder frozen and both denoisers trainable. The video and action branches receive separate clean-reconstruction MSE objectives, with the video prediction detached before action conditioning.

The reported configuration uses Cosmos-Predict2 2B-Video2World, 93 frames at 10 Hz, input resizing to 432×768, 16 latent channels and a 132-dimensional global embedding. General training is 40,000 iterations on eight NVIDIA H20 GPUs, batch size one per GPU; the LIBERO experiment instead reports 20,000 iterations.

AgiBot G1 uses 1,794 training and 200 test pairs with 16-dimensional actions. LIBERO uses 400 training and 50 test pairs selected across four suites, with seven-dimensional actions. Agilex data allocates 131 samples to VAG and 20 to VLA training, with 14-dimensional actions. Real datasets use head-camera video; LIBERO stitches head and wrist views.

inference.text: Initialize video and action noise, repeatedly predict a clean video latent and condition the action denoiser on its pooled embedding, then return decoded video and actions after 35 steps. The introduction's 'single feed-forward pass' wording should not be read as single-step generation.

Synthetic pairs pretrain a separate pi0.5 policy, which is subsequently fine-tuned on real demonstrations. Alternatively, VAG-generated trajectories are replayed on Agilex. The source describes generation followed by replay, without a documented feedback or replanning loop for VAG itself.

equations.explanation: Equations (1)–(3): x is a data sample, epsilon is Gaussian noise, and t is a logit-normal timestep in [0,1]. The interpolation x_t has target velocity v_t. The model u, parameterized by theta and conditioned on c, learns that velocity by squared error.

Equations (4)–(5) present clean-reconstruction losses: z and A are clean video latents and actions; primes mark noise-perturbed inputs. D and U are the DiT and U-Net with parameters theta_1 and theta_2; phi_1 and phi_2 reconstruct clean predictions. Conditioning is described in prose but omitted from these displayed function arguments.

results.setting: AgiBot G1 test split: 200 pairs; generation conditioned on first frame and corresponding prompt.
results.comparison: Cosmos-Predict2: 988, 135, 0.352, 0.427, 14.2. Wan2.2 leads FID (129) and SSIM (0.612).
results.interpretation: VAG leads three of five metrics. Video-quality scores do not measure executed action success; matched baseline post-training details are incomplete.

results.setting: AgiBot and LIBERO test pairs; two-stage baselines regress actions from VAG-generated videos.
results.metric: Euclidean distance (ED, lower) and threshold-based success rate (SR, higher)
results.value: VAG: AgiBot ED 0.81 / SR 45%; LIBERO ED 0.38 / SR 79%.
results.interpretation: SR requires error below 0.2 in every action dimension. It measures agreement with recorded actions, not environment task completion; normalization and temporal aggregation remain unspecified.

results.setting: Generated trajectories replayed in Spatial, Object, Goal and Long suites; trial counts and repeated-seed uncertainty are not specified.
results.value: VAG: Spatial 70, Object 72, Goal 64, Long 42; average 62.
results.interpretation: The reported average exceeds AnyPos by 8 percentage points, but Long remains weakest. This replay result is distinct from the 79% action-threshold score.

results.task: Real-robot tableware pick-and-place after synthetic pretraining
results.setting: Train VAG on 131 samples, generate X_syn, pretrain pi0.5 to convergence, then fine-tune on 20 real samples for 10,000 iterations; 20 deployment trials per policy.
results.comparison: pi0.5 trained on the 20 real samples for 10,000 iterations: 7/20 (35%).
results.interpretation: The gain is 20 percentage points, or four additional successes. This small study supports usefulness under the tested protocol; it lacks equal-compute and additional-real-data pretraining controls.

limitations.text: The authors identify one-way coupling as a limitation and propose action-guided video generation, a larger action DiT, more data and broader task evaluation as future work.

No controlled ablation isolates pooling, detachment or synchronized noise. Baseline comparisons change the action architecture and generation procedure together. Training-loss curves and selected trajectory overlays diagnose behavior but cannot identify the cause of improvement.

Global averaging discards explicit spatial and temporal positions in the conditioning vector. The source's strong alignment language is not a mathematical guarantee; Figure 9 visibly retains gripper-transition errors despite close arm-trajectory agreement.

The physical replay examples are selected demonstrations, not a VAG deployment success-rate study. The separate pi0.5 comparison has only 20 trials per condition, unspecified synthetic-set size and pretraining duration, and no reported uncertainty.

reproduction.text: Reproduction requires the stated model components, embodiment-specific data splits, camera preprocessing and replay interfaces. The PDF omits optimizer, learning rate, precise noise/guidance settings, software versions and exact action normalization; these must be resolved before interpreting ED or the 0.2 threshold.

The 16-to-132 channel-repetition rule is not fully specified. The relation between velocity MSE and clean-reconstruction MSE needs implementation clarification. A useful proposed check is to vary pooled conditioning while fixing denoisers and noise schedules; a second is to match pretraining compute and real-data exposure in the transfer comparison.

reasoning.text: The catalog is entirely unassigned, so there is no recorded quadrant to affirm or contradict. Architecture evidence supports joint future-video/action generation by two distinct denoisers, coupled through detached video conditioning. This is not sequential video-to-IDM extraction, but a unified framework does not establish a single shared backbone or a 'One Model' classification. Video prediction is used during action inference, not solely as a training auxiliary.

discussionQuestions: Would temporally structured conditioning reduce the gripper-transition errors visible in Figure 9?
Would the transfer advantage persist against equal-compute pretraining directly on the 131 real demonstrations?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, complete byline, affiliation block and arXiv margin stamp
evidence.detail: Title and all 13 authors match the catalog; the artifact is labeled arXiv:2604.09330v1 [cs.RO], 10 April 2026. Five affiliations are listed.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Section 1, motivation, proposed method and contribution bullets
evidence.detail: The authors motivate aligned synthetic training pairs, claim rigorous alignment and describe single-feed-forward generation; these are author claims to read alongside the iterative method.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Figure 3 and Section 3.2, Video Prediction
evidence.detail: The diagram shows image/text-conditioned video DiT, a decoder, pooling into a separate action U-Net, frozen encoder, trainable denoisers and a detach marker in training. Text specifies Cosmos-Predict2, noise scaling, T5-XXL and classifier-free guidance.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.2, continuation of Video Prediction and Action Prediction
evidence.detail: Each denoising step sends predicted clean video latents through global adaptive 3D average pooling and channel repetition to a time-conditioned 1D action U-Net; both finish after N steps.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.3, Video Branch and Action Branch, Equations (4)–(5)
evidence.detail: Training uses Qwen2.5-VL-derived instructions, T5-XXL, pretrained video weights, VAE compression of 4×8×8, clean-reconstruction losses and detached predicted-video conditioning with matched noise intensity.
Configuration: Cosmos-Predict2 2B-Video2World, 10 Hz, 93 frames, resize 432×768, C=3, C'=16, C''=132, 35 denoising steps; 40,000 iterations on eight H20 GPUs with batch size one per GPU.

Used splits are AgiBot G1 1,794/200 and LIBERO 400/50 training/test pairs; actions have 16 and 7 dimensions. Agilex allocates 131 VAG-training and 20 VLA-training samples with 14-dimensional actions; camera views are specified.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Table 1, all rows and metric columns; Section 4.2, video test inputs
evidence.detail: VAG reports FVD 965, FID 130, LPIPS 0.320, SSIM 0.512, PSNR 15.1. CP2 reports 988/135/0.352/0.427/14.2; Wan2.2 has best FID 129 and SSIM 0.612.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Table 2, all rows; p. 7, Section 4.2, action-evaluation paragraph
evidence.detail: VAG ED/SR is 0.81/45% for AgiBot and 0.38/79% for LIBERO; AnyPos is 0.98/29% and 0.55/66%; ResNet is 1.54/8% and 0.87/37%. Success is defined by error below 0.2 in every dimension.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Figure 4; p. 7, Section 4.3 and Figure 8
evidence.detail: AgiBot loss curves cover 40,000 iterations; LIBERO training and curves cover 20,000 iterations. These are optimization diagnostics, not component-removal comparisons.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Table 3, all rows; Section 4.3 continuation
evidence.detail: LIBERO replay success for VAG is 70/72/64/42, average 62; AnyPos 59/62/56/39, average 54; ResNet 33/34/23/10, average 25. This table reports replay rather than action-error thresholding.

VAG learns from X_a of 131 samples; synthetic pairs pretrain pi0.5 to convergence before 10,000-step fine-tuning on X_b of 20 samples. Real tableware trials yield 11/20 versus 7/20; figures illustrate relocation/color cases and loss/success comparisons.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Section 4.5; p. 9, Figure 12 and caption
evidence.detail: Head-camera image and instruction generate trajectories replayed on Agilex. Three selected examples cover left-arm, right-arm and bimanual manipulation; no aggregate VAG physical-replay success rate is supplied.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Limitations and Future Work
evidence.detail: Video generation currently receives no action-branch influence. Proposed extensions include reverse conditioning, replacing the action U-Net by a DiT, larger data and wider tasks.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section 3.1, Equations (1)–(2); p. 4, Equation (3) and symbol definitions
evidence.detail: Flow matching interpolates data and Gaussian noise using a logit-normal timestep; the target velocity is noise minus data, trained by conditional velocity squared error.
SVD and Wan2.2 video baselines have 1.5B and 5B parameters. Action baselines use ResNet50 plus MLPs or AnyPos to regress actions from VAG videos and are trained for 40,000 iterations.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Figure 9, axes, GT Action/Pred Action legend and caption
evidence.detail: The selected LIBERO bowl-to-plate example overlays six arm-action channels and a gripper channel over frames. Arm curves largely overlap; predicted gripper transitions are smoother and overshoot the ground-truth steps. No action units or component ablation are shown.
